title: What If Your Gut Brewed Its Own Alcohol? One Man Blew 0.2% With No Drinks

scenes.text: What if your gut brewed its own alcohol? For a few people, it does. Ask the police.
In 2019, doctors described a 46-year-old man arrested for drunk driving. Blood alcohol: 0.2 percent. He swore he hadn't touched a drink.
Stool tests found brewer's yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, living in his intestines.
Every carbohydrate meal became a fermentation. In hospital, his level once climbed to 0.4 percent, from bread and pizza.
It had started in 2011, right after a three-week course of antibiotics, which likely cleared the way for the yeast.
Antifungal drugs, probiotics and six weeks without carbs finally shut the brewery down. Doctors call it auto-brewery syndrome, and they think it's underdiagnosed.

description:
What if your gut brewed its own alcohol? Auto-brewery syndrome is real: yeast in the gut ferments carbohydrates into ethanol.
A 2019 case report in BMJ Open Gastroenterology described a 46-year-old man arrested for drunk driving with a blood alcohol level of 0.2 percent despite not drinking; brewer's yeast was found in his gut, levels reached 0.4 percent in hospital, and antifungal treatment plus a low-carb diet cleared it.
What should we run through next?
first_comment: The yeast took over after antibiotics wiped out his normal gut bacteria. Would you believe a friend who said their stomach made them drunk? And what should we run through next?
